title: The self comes in at the crown
hookLine: the house is full of gods, and the self asks a strange question: if all of them do all the work, then who am I?
carry: atman: the one who sees through every door

cards: Here's a company where every department runs perfectly. Speech does the talking. Breath does the breathing.

The eyes see, the ears hear, the mind thinks. Then the founder walks through the building with an uncomfortable thought: if they all do everything, what am I for? That's where the Aitareya's first chapter ends.
The self has made worlds, a person, a house full of gods and appetites. Now it looks at all that working machinery and asks how it could possibly be there without itself.

teach.h: IF THEY DO EVERYTHING, WHO AM I?
teach.b: The text gives the self two questions. How could this be without me? And: by which way shall I enter?
Then comes a list, almost comic. If speaking is done by speech, breathing by breath, seeing by the eye, hearing by the ear, thinking by the mind, then who am I? So the self finds its own door.
Not the mouth, the nostrils or the eyes; those were taken.

teach.h: THE SELF SPLITS THE SEAM AT THE CROWN.
teach.b: It splits open the seam at the very top of the skull, where the bones meet, and enters there. The text names that door vidriti, the cleft, and calls it the place of joy. Every other god came in through a working opening.
The self comes in through a door that does nothing at all. It doesn't speak, see or breathe. It's just the way in.
Once inside, the self looks around and sees this very person as Brahman, spread out everywhere. Idam adarsham, it says.
Here is one of Hinduism's central teachings: atman, the self. Not the eyes, not the voice, not the mind's chatter, but the one who sees through all of them.
Later yoga traditions name a point at the crown, the brahmarandhra, and some readers connect it to this passage. The Aitareya's point is simpler. Your talents and senses are doors.
You are the one who came in to see. So on the day one door shuts, a lost voice, a hurt knee, a test that went badly, the self hasn't gone anywhere.

how: Some Hindu men, especially in priestly families, keep a tuft of hair, the shikha, near the crown, and some yoga and meditation teachers direct attention to the crown of the head, which later texts call the brahmarandhra.

o: the cleft at the crown where the self enters
the heart, where the moon becomes mind
the mouth, where fire enters as speech

games.q: the self's question — tap the pairs.
p: the cleft: a place of joy

s: the self enters through the eyes, like the sun
the sun took the eyes. the self splits the seam at the crown.
the self asks, 'how could this be without me?'
then it asks which way to enter, and finds the door at the top.
the Aitareya uses the word brahmarandhra
the text says vidriti, the cleft. brahmarandhra is from later yoga traditions.

games.q: your grandfather's eyes and ears are fading. he says, 'i'm disappearing a little every year.' what would the Aitareya say?
o: he is: the self lives in the senses, so it fades with them.
the senses are doors the gods came through; the self, atman, is the one who sees through them.
only the mind is the self, so as long as he thinks clearly he's fine.
games.why: each god took a working door; the self came in by a door that does nothing, and saw. the doors can close. the one who sees isn't one of them.

practice: Sit tall and let your attention rest on the crown of your head, where the seams of the skull meet: air, warmth, the weight of your hair, or nothing much.
This spot isn't talking or watching or breathing, and still something is aware of it. Rest in that awareness, the one that came in by the quiet door.

wordCard.voice: Vidriti, the cleft at the crown of the head where the self enters. In the Aitareya, after every god has its door, the self comes in through this door, and sees.

orig.note: Sanskrit vidṛti, the cleft: the door at the crown where the self enters, Aitareya 1.3.12.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: atman, the one who sees through every door. Tomorrow, the Aitareya counts births. Day four hundred two.

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 1.3.11–1.3.14 (the self enters at the crown; three dwellings; 'I have seen this')
